Newton defines quantity of motion as the product of a body's mass and its velocity; force is that which changes this quantity—either resisting or impressing motion.

1) A body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by an impressed force. 2) The change of motion is proportional to the impressed force and occurs in its direction. 3) For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. In celestial mechanics, these laws explain orbital persistence, gravitational acceleration, and mutual perturbations among bodies.

He shows that a body under a central (centripetal) force sweeps out equal areas in equal times because the force always acts along the radius, altering direction but preserving area–time proportionality.
He proves that the centripetal force required for circular motion varies as 1/(radius²), and by applying that to planetary orbits, he establishes gravity’s inverse-square relationship.
He observes that all bodies fall toward Earth at the same rate and that planets mutually perturb one another—indicating a universal attractive force acting between every pair of masses.

He notes that besides the Sun’s dominant pull, each planet exerts smaller centripetal forces on the others, causing slight deviations from perfect ellipses that can be calculated from their masses and distances.

He employed the method of fluxions and infinite series to compute rates of change and areas, but he presented results through classical geometric proofs to ensure rigor, avoiding symbolic calculus notation.

He defines centripetal force as that which continually turns a body from its straight-line path toward a center, and shows that such a force—gravity—produces curved orbits with area–time proportionality.
He demonstrates that resisting media retard motion in proportion to velocity or its square, and he provides geometric constructions to correct projectile and celestial motions for such resistance.

He distinguishes absolute time, which flows uniformly on its own, and absolute space, which remains fixed and immovable, from relative measures; these absolutes provide the unchanging reference frame needed for his laws.
Robert Newton.
Beyond his grandfather Robert, family tradition suggests Scottish origins or ties to Newton in Lancashire, but no further lineage is confirmed.
